angle: The combo sheet claims nineteen two-card infinites and exactly one case file has ever signed one — so this issue teaches you to run the near-certain turn-2 mint underneath that ceiling, and to be the only visible threat at a table that has not yet decided to care.

cover.dominant_coverline: THE LOOP THAT MAKES NO MANA
teases: Mikaeus + Devoted Druid: four counter placements and one death per cycle, forever, at zero mana
Feed a Snake token to undying and nothing comes back — six famous pairings die on the same page
Turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs: the one card your opening seven never has to find
Two boards, your call — the two-mana turn, and the famous loop against the checked one

departments.note: Full-bleed Hapatra art crop, masthead trio, identity block verbatim from issue.json. Both violators are delivered inside: the six refuted pairings in The Kill and Judge's Desk, the zero-tapped base in Sources Say.
Five-act Flight Plan, promises verbatim from issue_spec, tier legend and columnist bios printed in full — first-issue reader assumed.

departments.headline: THE TWO-MANA GUARANTEE
departments.dek: What is the command zone actually worth to you? Here it is worth a two-mana legend on turn two in 9,970 of 10,000 runs — a guarantee so cheap it rewrites what your opening seven has to find. The Counselor reads the fine print; the Coach reads the table.
departments.body:
Begin with the exhibit everyone skips: the zone itself. Rule 903.4 seats Hapatra there before a card is drawn, and she may be cast from it any time you could cast a sorcery. She costs two. The seeded runs put her on the battlefield on turn two 9,970 times out of 10,000, mean cast turn 2.007.

The holding follows, and it inverts your mulligan. Your opening seven never has to contain her. All seven cards are free to hunt the one thing the zone cannot promise — a repeatable way to put -1/-1 counters on a creature.

Read the ladder above against this deck's ledger. Rule 903.8 charges {2} more on every return trip, and mean available mana is 4.71 on turn four and 6.15 on turn six. A second cast at four is on schedule. A third at six is a turn, not a tragedy.

So the court's spending advice is blunt: for Hapatra, pay the tax. Keep Heroic Intervention and the boots for Yawgmoth and Mikaeus — the pieces the zone does not hand back.

Colour identity is the clause with teeth, and 903.4 counts mana symbols in rules text, not just costs. Black-green admits every -1/-1 counter card on the record and forbids the counterspell outright.

Note what it does not forbid. Green owns artifact and enchantment removal, and this 99 carries none of it. That hole is a signed trade, not a legal constraint — say so plainly in your Rule 0 conversation.

On the 21-damage clock, 903.10a, the record is short. Hapatra is an unevasive 2/2, and eleven successful combats against one defender is not a plan. The file classifies her combat trigger as a bonus, never an engine. The clock exists. It is not yours.

Coach's corner. Here is the strange seat this commander puts you in: you are the only player with a permanent doing work on turn two, and nobody is looking at you. Visible and boring at once. Bank every turn that read buys you, and expect it revoked the first time a tutor resolves.

captions.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: **THE GUARANTEE:** two mana, both colours, every single game — the one card your mulligan never has to go looking for.

pilot_tips.text: Spend Opal Palace's mana on a taxed recast and Hapatra returns wearing +1/+1 counters — the answer to a table that keeps killing her cheaply.

departments.pull_quote: The zone promises her. Your seven cards are free to promise everything else.

departments.headline: RUN THE MINT
departments.dek: Why does a 2/2 that should never attack keep winning long games? Because Hapatra is a mint, not an engine. Other cards place the counters; she pays you a 1/1 deathtouch Snake per placement, and every Snake becomes a card or a life off all three seats.

callouts.title: LAND THE MINT
callouts.text: Two mana, turn two, 9,970 runs out of 10,000. Stop deliberating over turn two and spend that thinking on turn three, where the game actually forks.

callouts.title: HUNT THE SOURCE
callouts.text: The scarce class is two cards deep — Yawgmoth, Thran Physician, and Devoted Druid once Mikaeus is out. Eight tutors exist to fix exactly that. Source first, payoff second, every time.

callouts.title: CASH THE BODIES
callouts.text: Skullclamp, Grim Haruspex, Deadly Dispute and Village Rites turn a stream of 1/1s into a stream of cards. Out-card three opponents first; a drain converter is in hand in 51.9% of games, and it closes after you have counted their interaction.

pilot_tips.text: Spend Fume Spitter on the turn it does three jobs at once — a Snake, a dead X/1, and a body for a sacrifice cost.

captions.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: **THE MINT:** one Snake per placement event, not per counter — Black Sun's Zenith for one across six creatures mints six Snakes; three counters on one creature mints one.
captions.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: **THE SOURCE:** the only free repeatable -1/-1 source in the 99 — and his ability names one target, so aim at a creature that is not the one you just ate or you lose the counter and the card together.

departments.pull_quote: She does not make the counters. She sets the exchange rate.

departments.headline: RANK AND VILE
departments.dek: Sixty-four spells sort into one scarce class and a great deal of abundance behind it. The sources lead this roster because they have to — everything after them is bodies becoming cards, and cards becoming a clock on every seat.

roster.role: The sources — the class that is two deep
The converters — a clock on every seat

cards: Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER // Sephiroth, One-Winged Angel

roster.role: The ceiling — one case file, eleven open questions
Protection, recursion and the odd jobs

captions.Skullclamp: **THE ECONOMY:** every token here is a 1/1, so this reads as pay {1}, draw two, on repeat — the card that makes losing your board profitable.
captions.Obelisk Spider: **THE FAST CONVERTER:** it drains on counter placement rather than on death, which prices a loop roughly four times faster than any dies-trigger does.
captions.Nest of Scarabs: **THE EXCHANGE RATE:** your counters come back as that many 1/1 Insects — but only when you are the one placing them. Read the templating before you count on it.

pilot_tips.text: Mind the shroud: Greaves protects the Druid and locks Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting it, so decide which you want before you equip.

departments.headline: ROUTE OR RERACK
departments.dek: Now that you have read the roster, the keep test is one question: does this hand reach a repeatable counter source? Ledger's receipts say you keep 79.9% of first sevens and average 0.243 mulligans — so you can afford to be picky, and you should be.

hands.why: Three lands, a turn-one dork, the one free repeatable source in the 99, and two ways to cash it. Hapatra waits in the zone — this hand is holding the card the zone cannot promise.

A two-lander carries when a dork comes with it, and Demonic Tutor is any card you like. Keep Blowfly Infestation for what it reliably is — a counter source for the grind — and never as half of a kill nobody has signed off on.

Four lands, three converters, nothing that places a counter. The goldfish keeps this hand because its rule only counts lands, and you are smarter than the goldfish: these are blanks waiting on a card you have not drawn.

hands.verdict: SHIP — one land and a prayer
hands.why: A Petal that finds no second land costs you the commander, and Mikaeus is the only six-drop in the deck — a piece for two named partners, not a plan. Mean mulligans run 0.243, and shipping this is what that average is made of.

pilot_tips.text: Count Lotus Petal as a spell you are owed, not a land you have — a mox hand with one land is still a ship.

captions.Bitterblossom: **THE FREE KEEP:** a body every upkeep for one life, rebuilding through a wrath on its own — this is a keepable engine all by itself.

departments.headline: TWO BOARDS, YOUR CALL
departments.dek: Two real turns, and the Coach's call is sealed under each. Turn two, three two-drops live, and a control player who has held two lands through their whole turn. Then turn five, six mana, and two infinite loops in hand — one famous, one checked. Commit before you scroll.

callouts.title: COMMIT OUT LOUD
callouts.text: Say your branch before you read ours. A call you make silently is a call you get to rewrite afterwards, and rewriting is how a habit never forms.

callouts.title: PRICE WHAT YOU LOSE
callouts.text: Each branch has a specific cost if the seat with mana up is holding what you think it is. Name that cost inside every branch first, then compare. Comparing upside against upside is how a good turn gets picked for the wrong reason.

departments.pull_quote: Both of these turns are decided by a player who has done absolutely nothing.

departments.headline: THE LOOP THAT MAKES NO MANA
departments.dek: Nineteen two-card infinites are claimed for this deck. One case file has been opened, and it affirms a loop that runs forever while producing exactly zero mana — then strikes six famous pairings off the sheet in the same breath.

callouts.title: FIRST PASS PAYS
callouts.text: The turn Mikaeus and Devoted Druid meet, the untap nets three green. Every pass after that nets none — the returned Druid is a new object and 302.6 silences its tap ability. The loop runs anyway, because the untap cost carries no tap symbol at all.

callouts.title: THE STEADY STATE
callouts.text: Four -1/-1 placements and one death per cycle, at zero mana. With Hapatra out that is four Snakes a cycle. With Obelisk Spider it is four table-wide drains. With Blood Artist, one life per cycle from a player of your choosing.

callouts.title: THE THIRD CARD
callouts.text: Mikaeus plus Walking Ballista is real and it is three cards, not two. The anthem holds a counterless Ballista at 1/1, so it will not kill itself and an external free outlet is mandatory. With one, the damage is unbounded and no drain payoff is needed.

callouts.title: THE STRIKEOUTS
callouts.text: Six listed pairings die on the record. Both altars, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni and Blasting Station each buy exactly one undying return. Feed the loop a Snake token instead and you get zero — the token stops existing before its own undying trigger ever reaches the stack.

callouts.title: THE ONE THAT LOOPS ANYWAY
callouts.text: Yawgmoth loops for real with no Mikaeus in the picture, bounded by the library his own mandatory draw empties. A life and a body per activation, a card each time, a Snake each time. That is the kill you will actually cash.

captions.Devoted Druid: **EXHIBIT A:** the untap ability pays a -1/-1 counter as a cost and carries no tap symbol, so summoning sickness never touches it. That technicality is the entire infinite.
captions.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: **THE HINGE:** undying powers both affirmed lines — and the same anthem may switch your own token loops off, which is the largest question still open in this deck.
captions.Walking Ballista: **THE CLOSER:** unbounded alongside Mikaeus and any free outlet, and never a two-card kill, because the anthem will not let it shoot itself to death.

pilot_tips.text: Equip Greaves to restore four green a cycle, and accept that its shroud locks Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting the wearer.

departments.pull_quote: The sheet said nineteen. The file says one true infinite, six strikeouts, and eleven questions nobody has answered.
departments.note: The renderer emits the dossier pointer to Case A-001 itself; the callouts above carry the findings, and the verbatim citations stay in Judge's Desk.

departments.headline: FIRST ON THE BOARD, LAST ON THE LIST
departments.dek: You are the only player with a permanent doing work on turn two, in 9,970 runs out of 10,000 — so why does nobody point anything at you? Because a 2/2 and a spread of 1/1 Snakes reads as furniture. How long that read survives is a sequencing decision, and it is yours.

callouts.title: THE COVER
callouts.text: Deathtouch Snakes read as defence, and they are — every attacker trades down into a token that cost you nothing. Lead with the token half and the cheap counter sources, and let three opponents keep filing you under later.

callouts.title: THE TELL
callouts.text: Eleven Game Changers live in this list. The moment a Mox, a Demonic Tutor or The One Ring resolves, the Snakes stop reading as chump blockers. Fire the loud cards on turns that convert, and on turns a louder seat has just done something.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: The flip to archenemy is never Hapatra. It is the second permanent: Yawgmoth with a spare body, or Mikaeus beside Devoted Druid or Walking Ballista. Go on the turn you are protected, or do not go.

pilot_tips.text: Cast The One Ring on the turn you want the cards, never on the turn you want the protection to look clever — it is the loudest card you own.

captions.Orcish Bowmasters: **THE QUIET MENACE:** flash it in on somebody else's draw spell — rare instant-speed interaction that spends none of your cover.

departments.pull_quote: The table is not wrong to fear your second permanent. Make sure it is the last thing they see coming.

departments.headline: DEATHTOUCH IS A POLICY
departments.dek: Aggro cannot attack into you and midrange cannot out-grind you — so which board should actually frighten you? The one with no creatures on it and a Winter Orb. Rank threats by permanent class before you rank them by size.

threats.read: Your interaction covers exactly one permanent class, and it is not theirs. A resolved Sphere, Orb or hoser stays resolved, so you race it or you politick it. Two things genuinely favour you: your engines cost no mana once assembled, and your commander lands on turn two, so you can often be under the lock before the second and third pieces layer. Then trade with the truth — say out loud that you have no answer, and ask the seat holding the removal to spend it.

You can only interact with creature-based kills, and against combo a held answer rots — the last profitable moment is now. Do not plan to out-race a dedicated combo deck either: your own headline assembly runs 16.3% at mean turn 4.10 and nobody has adjudicated it. Be the seat their interaction is not pointed at, and remember your Game Changers spend that cover fast.

Your token half is nearly free to lose. Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep, Skullclamp and Grim Haruspex cash the deaths, and a wrath with Blood Artist out is a drain you get to aim. The half that wins is all creatures, though, so deploy in waves and hold the enabler until the pivot. Know your own sweepers apart: Black Sun's Zenith is a rebuild that mints Snakes, and Toxic Deluge places nothing and feeds nobody.

A 1/1 deathtouch Snake blanks an attacker of any size, and a board of them blanks three attack plans at once — the cheapest answer to roughly 120 life of aggression ever printed. Track the one clock that is actually real and defend against that seat only. Spend life on purpose here; this deck already treats it as a resource.

The seat this deck was built for. Their removal is bad against tokens, their attacks are bad into deathtouch, and Crumbling Ashes beside any counter source is repeating removal that fair decks mostly cannot touch. Out-card them with the bodies-into-cards layer, then pivot on a counted window rather than a pretty board.

pilot_tips.text: Sequence Toxic Deluge as the panic button it is — until-end-of-turn -X/-X places no counters, so it mints nothing and feeds nobody.

departments.pull_quote: An answer only counts when it matches a threat that actually beats you.

departments.headline: SAME WISH, EIGHT LAMPS
departments.dek: Why do eight tutors keep naming the same card? Because the class that wins the game is two cards deep, and a two-deep class with eight finders plays like a deep one. You draw a tutor in 78.0% of games at mean turn 2.695 — so learn the delivery speeds before you fire one.

pilot_tips.text: Fire Vampiric Tutor at the end step before your untap — the wish spends no turns in transit and nobody gets a draw step to answer it.

captions.Green Sun's Zenith: **THE TEMPO WISH:** the only tutor here that pays tempo instead of charging it — Devoted Druid arrives on the battlefield, not in your hand.

departments.pull_quote: The tutors can make you faster. Nothing in this 99 can make you broader.

departments.headline: THIRTY-SIX LANDS, NONE TAPPED
departments.dek: How lopsided can a pip load get before the mana breaks? Black carries 71.4% of the pips on a 50% source share and pays nothing for it — 29 black sources and 29 green against a target of 22 apiece, on curve 96.2% of the time on lands alone. Not one land in this deck arrives tapped.

captions.City of Brass: **THE INVOICE:** a base this clean is billed to your life total — City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel all charge you to fix.

pilot_tips.text: Point a spare -1/-1 counter at the Spirit you just handed away — the Orchard's tax comes back to you as a Snake.

departments.pull_quote: Twenty-two of these lands answer to either question. There is no split left to get wrong.

departments.headline: THE 2.007 COMMANDER
departments.dek: Mean cast turn 2.007. Hapatra is on the table before most decks have finished introducing themselves — and the rest of this ledger is about what happens next, and about what a simulation is not.

callouts.title: THE HEADLINE
callouts.text: Turn two in 9,970 of 10,000 runs, 99.9% by turn six. She is the most reliable card in the book, which is exactly why the plan never spends a thought on her.

callouts.title: THE REAL IDENTITY
callouts.text: Commander plus any -1/-1 payoff assembles in 67.2% of runs at mean turn 3.62, and 55.7% of runs have it by turn six. That pair is the deck — the grindy median that out-cards three opponents.

callouts.title: THE HONEST CEILING
callouts.text: Hapatra plus Blowfly Infestation: 16.3% assembled, 12.5% by turn six, and unadjudicated. Mikaeus plus a free outlet: 9.5%. The ceiling is real, it is narrow, and it is never the thing you mulligan toward.

departments.pull_quote: The model has no removal in it and no opponents worth the name. It still cannot stop casting her on turn two.

departments.headline: SCOUTED, NOT SIGNED
departments.dek: There is no bench behind this list, so all ten are pool scouts — eleven thousand seven hundred and ninety-nine eligible cards, ten through the gate. Four of them aim at the same hole, three route around a component that is one card deep, and not one of them moves the bracket.

pilot_tips.text: Do not wait for a scout to fix Blowfly Infestation — the pool search returned nothing that shares its job, so play it as a counter source and stop there.

departments.pull_quote: Every line these ten would open arrives wearing the same stamp — needs a stack scenario — because six lines that read this well on paper are already struck.

departments.headline: CASE A-001, READ TWICE
departments.dek: One seductive claim — that Hapatra's counter resets undying under Mikaeus — sixteen resolution steps and four review cycles, verdict: pass. Every citation below is verbatim. The claim is false as written, and what the file found instead is worth more than the claim ever was.
departments.pull_quote: Where the record is silent, the record is silent. Eleven listed lines remain open, and not one of them may be spoken of as fact.

departments.headline: EIGHTY HANDS
departments.dek: Nobody painted this deck. Eighty artists share its 88 cards and no one holds more than three — so the credit goes to the whole field, led by the man who happened to paint both the signature sweeper and the affirmed kill piece.

featured.note:
Daniel Ljunggren tops this roster with three cards, and in an eighty-artist field that is not a signature — it is the crest of a perfectly flat wave. John Avon also has three. Nobody else clears two. The analysis says it plainly: no standout, so the honest feature is the breadth itself.

That breadth has a cause worth saying out loud. Nobody chose these printings. The decklist names cards, not editions, so each entry carries whatever printing the resolver returned — which is why the largest single stamp on the deck is one Commander product holding twelve cards by twelve different artists, and why there is not one foil among the 88. No curation happened here, and we are not going to invent taste that nobody exercised.

What chance delivered is still worth the page. Ljunggren's three are Black Sun's Zenith, Forbidden Orchard and Walking Ballista — the deck's signature sweeper, its most mischievous land, and the piece the case file affirmed. If one set of hands had to lead a flat field, the ledger could have done far worse.

also_worth_noting.note: Opal Palace and Spire of Industry are classic Avon architecture. Serrated Arrows is the odd one out — even the utility slot gets a landscape painter here.
Two cards, maximum gravity: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed, the hinge of the whole issue, and Eternal Witness, the rebuy that keeps the engine honest.
Chrome Mox and Worldly Tutor — two of the eleven Game Changers, one brush.

captions.Black Sun's Zenith: **THE SIGNATURE PIECE:** Ljunggren's sweeper is the card this deck's whole economy runs through — X counters on each creature, one Snake per creature.

rhythm_notes: Act I meets the deck and climbs: The Command Zone opens on instruction at medium intensity because it is the reader's first contact, The Game Plan takes the narrative high, and The 99 drops to browsing so the roster is a rest rather than a wall. Act II flies it — practice, then active participation across two decision spreads, then The Kill as the mid-book peak and the payoff for all three. Act III is three consecutive Coach sections and deliberately alternates mode: reflection, reference, instruction. Act IV is three consecutive Ledger ones, and its only dense adjacency, Sources Say into By the Numbers, is the declared art break the renderer emits. The Short List cools to imagination, so Judge's Desk arrives buffered by imagination before and appreciation after. Nothing dense sits adjacent undeclared.
gaps: Eleven of the nineteen claimed two-card infinites have no case file. Highest value first: does Mikaeus's anthem switch the Blowfly and Hapatra token loops off — if it does, the deck's two flagship engines are mutually exclusive on the battlefield. Then the Blowfly family itself, which decision 002 hands the reader as an unadjudicated branch and which the goldfish tracks at 16.3%.

Yawgmoth plus Hapatra without Mikaeus is very likely the line this deck wins with most often, and it has no scenario. It needs one: the target-survives requirement, the single-target fizzle, and the life-and-library bound.

Three more worth a scenario: Scurry Oak plus Ivy Lane Denizen (the bracket report's highest-bracket line, and the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries that look like the same projection artifact), Hapatra plus Host of the Hereafter, and Necroskitter alongside Black Sun's Zenith as a one-sided wipe-and-steal.

One rules question the tutor guide already flags and plays around: whether Heroic Intervention saves a creature being killed by toughness reduction rather than destruction. Fetch Quests currently tells the reader to assume it does not.

Strategy DB topics the frame names as missing: auditing a combo list, the aristocrats outlet/fodder/converter taxonomy, counters-matter fundamentals including the anthem-versus-shrink anti-synergy, in-game tutor sequencing, and when a fast-mana trade is correct.
